title: ProtonVPN Automation in 2026: Setup Steps and Fixes
summary: ProtonVPN automation uses auto-connect, kill switch, and Linux command line, not an API. You'll learn what automation capabilities are genuinely available.
body_markdown:
## Cost of a dropped ProtonVPN tunnel


With the kill switch off, the dropped tunnel cost four things, and none of them raised an error: lost work hours, devices running unprotected, logins to rotate, and support time.


I have no measured counts for this case, so what follows is the ledger's structure, not its totals.


### Work hours lost to VPN failure


Reproduce it the same way each time: the tunnel drops, auto-connect doesn't bring it back, and the app still shows a normal-looking state. Nobody files a ticket for that.


People notice only when an internal resource stops loading, and by then the gap has stayed open for an unknown stretch.


Log three timestamps per incident: when the tunnel dropped, when someone noticed, and when someone fixed it. The span between the first two is the real loss, because it's time spent working on an unprotected connection without knowing it.


Multiply it across everyone affected and the quiet failure stops looking quiet.


### Devices exposed when ProtonVPN drops


Count devices, not people. Each device that sent traffic outside the tunnel while the kill switch was off is one entry, and a person with a laptop and a phone is two.


The plan's simultaneous-connection limit matters here: a device that was never connected because the limit was hit counts as unprotected just like one whose tunnel dropped.


Then list every login used on those devices during the gap. Each one goes on the rotation list, because without a kill switch you can't prove the traffic stayed private. Assume exposure, rotate the credential, and record the time that took.
